strengths: The concept of 'Causal Pathways' (CPs) provides a structured and deterministic approach to GUI evaluation, where failure at an intermediate atomic step triggers an unambiguous failure signal and isolates the root cause.

The multi-level evaluation metrics (WPSR, MATCR, p-ATSR, and detailed error categorization into KD, PE, OE, PRE, SCE) offer fine-grained diagnostic insight into GUI agent failures beyond simple binary task success.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across modern proprietary and open-source models (including Gemini, Claude, and Qwen series), accompanied by out-of-domain transfer evaluation on the A3 benchmark.
weaknesses: The description of Trajectory-Reinforced Fine-Tuning (T-RFT) in Section 4.4 lacks essential technical details in the main text; it is conceptually described as bridging SFT and RL, but the concrete optimization objective, loss formulation, and policy update mechanism are omitted.

The benchmark relies on live third-party applications and web services (e.g., IMDb, Douban, Wikipedia). Dynamic interface updates and live web content shifts pose significant risks to long-term reproducibility and deterministic programmatic verification unless strictly mocked or sandboxed.

Experimental setup and baseline fairness for cross-platform tasks are unclear: baseline agents (PC-Agent and Mobile-Agent-e) are designed for single operating systems, leaving it ambiguous how they were adapted or evaluated on multi-device, cross-platform workflows compared to the natively multi-agent LightManus.

The scale of both the benchmark (276 tasks) and the trajectory dataset (523 trajectories) is relatively modest, and the exact relationship/overlap between the trajectory training set and the evaluation benchmark needs more transparent documentation to rule out data leakage.

strengths: The conceptual formulation of Causal Pathways (CPs) provides a principled way to decompose complex GUI workflows into causally-dependent atomic tasks, enabling deterministic failure detection ('Path Collapse') rather than relying purely on end-state LLM-as-a-judge evaluators.

The multi-level evaluation framework is thorough and well-designed, offering macro metrics (WPSR), progress metrics (MATCR, p-ATSR), and a detailed error taxonomy (PRE, SCE, OE, KD, PE) that provides deep diagnostic insights into agent failures.

Extensive experimental benchmarking across an impressive array of frontier proprietary and open-source models (Claude-sonnet-4, GPT-o3, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Qwen family), providing realistic and challenging baselines where even top models achieve <35% WPSR.

The curated dataset explicitly captures self-correction and recovery trajectories rather than only optimal paths, and testing out-of-domain transfer on the A3 benchmark validates generalization benefits.
weaknesses: Critical implementation details of the Trajectory-Reinforced Fine-Tuning (T-RFT) method are omitted from the main text; Section 4.4 only discusses T-RFT conceptually without any mathematical formulation, loss functions, or optimization algorithms (deferring details to an unavailable Appendix C).

The programmatic verification mechanism is insufficiently explained; while the authors claim atomic steps have programmatically verifiable answers across diverse platforms (Android and Windows), the paper does not specify how environment states and answers are verified deterministically without manual checks or LLM judges.

The benchmark scale is relatively modest (276 total tasks across three difficulty levels), and the trajectory generation relies primarily on a single model (Gemini-2.5-Pro) across 265 atomic tasks, which may introduce model-specific behavioral biases into the curated dataset.

LightManus primarily integrates existing components (Mobile-Agent-e for Android and PC-Agent for desktop) under a high-level task parser and workflow manager, making the architectural contribution relatively incremental.

strengths: Principled Benchmark Design: The concept of 'Causal Pathways'—decomposing long-horizon GUI workflows into verifiable, causally dependent atomic steps where failure induces deterministic path collapse—effectively tackles the unreliability and cost of MLLM-as-a-judge and open-ended final-state verification.

Diagnostic Multi-Level Evaluation: The evaluation framework incorporates macro-level completion (WPSR), progress/traversal metrics (MATCR, p-ATSR), and granular failure attribution (Planning & Reasoning, Structural Compliance, Knowledge Deficits, Perceptual, and Operational errors), providing informative diagnostic insights into agent bottlenecks.
Cross-Platform Workflow Integration: The benchmark models complex realistic tasks requiring orchestration across both mobile (Android) and desktop (PC) environments.

Insightful Empirical Findings: The empirical evaluation across several state-of-the-art closed and open-source models yields useful observations, particularly that fine-tuning smaller models (7B) on GUI trajectories provides local operational improvements but fails to overcome long-horizon reasoning and planning ceilings.
weaknesses: Lack of Technical and Algorithmic Rigor for T-RFT: Although Trajectory-Reinforced Fine-Tuning (T-RFT) is highlighted as one of the paper's three main contributions, Section 4.4 lacks any mathematical formalization, loss functions, reward definitions, or algorithmic pseudocode explaining how policy optimization was performed on static offline trajectories.

Limited Benchmark and Dataset Scale: The benchmark consists of only 276 tasks, and the curated trajectory dataset contains 523 trajectories (with only 278 used for fine-tuning). Given the vast action spaces and diversity of cross-platform apps, this scale is relatively small and limits statistical robustness across sub-categories.

Environmental Reproducibility Concerns: The paper tests on live, evolving real-world platforms (e.g., Douban, IMDb, Wikipedia). Dynamic online content and interface updates can cause programmatic checks and ground-truth answers to drift over time, an issue that is not sufficiently addressed with mock or sandboxed environment setups.

Incremental Agent Architecture: LightManus largely acts as a standard hierarchical orchestrator delegating sub-tasks to existing modules (Mobile-Agent-e and PC-Agent); the architectural contribution is relatively engineering-heavy and incremental compared to prior hierarchical agent systems.

Omission of Crucial Details in the Main Text: Several important operational details—such as the exact positional weighting function p(i) for p-ATSR, the dataset split between training trajectories and benchmark tasks, and baseline prompting protocols—are omitted from the main body.

strengths: Addresses a critical bottleneck in GUI agent benchmarking: the tension between natural, ambiguous user instructions and deterministic, reproducible evaluation without relying on noisy LLM judges.

The benchmark generation methodology—grounding multi-hop causal paths in Wikidata triples and wrapping them in naturalized narratives—provides a principled, path-invariant evaluation protocol combining both UI state checks and answer verification.
Introduces well-formulated, fine-grained evaluation metrics (MATCR, p-ATSR, WPSR) that quantify partial execution progress and long-horizon degradation beyond simple binary success rates.

The LightManus-Jarvis hierarchical architecture is well-motivated and demonstrates substantial empirical gains in success rate (45.6% WPSR vs. 21.1% baseline) alongside massive reductions in token consumption (~75%) and execution time (~76%).

Extensive experimental evaluation across diverse model families (Gemini, Claude, GPT, Qwen) and difficulty tiers, supported by thorough error categorization and cross-benchmark testing on AndroidWorld.
weaknesses: Benchmark task distribution leans heavily on entity-centric knowledge retrieval chains (e.g., finding actors, musicians, or historical facts across Wikipedia, IMDb, and Spotify) rather than transactional, open-ended productivity workflows (e.g., setting configurations, form filling, complex document handling).

The baseline comparisons in Table 2 conflate architectural improvements with differences in observation modalities; Jarvis utilizes structured accessibility trees (UID-based coordinate-free actions), whereas key baselines like Mobile-Agent-e rely solely on vision, naturally confounding perceptual error rates with planning capabilities.
The benchmark size is relatively small (276 tasks), and expanding it remains constrained by the required human-in-the-loop verification protocol for solvability and consistency checks.

strengths: Addresses a fundamental bottleneck in GUI agent evaluation (the 'Evaluation-Realism Dilemma') by proposing a logico-linguistic decoupling methodology grounded in Wikidata causal paths, providing verifiable ground truth alongside natural, non-linear instructions.

Proposes informative, fine-grained diagnostic metrics (MATCR, p-ATSR, and error attribution) that move beyond standard binary task success to evaluate intermediate progress and long-horizon trajectory coherence.

The proposed LightManus-Jarvis framework effectively demonstrates the value of a macro-planning and micro-execution decoupling, yielding substantial token reductions (approx. 75%) and latency improvements compared to monolithic mobile GUI agents.
Extensive experimental evaluation across diverse task difficulties and multiple proprietary and open-source foundation model backends, complemented by cross-benchmark validation on AndroidWorld.
weaknesses: The evaluation setup contains confounding modality differences across baselines: Jarvis relies on hybrid perception (Screenshot + Android Accessibility XML tree), whereas primary baselines like Mobile-Agent-e and PC-Agent are pure vision-based, making it difficult to fully disentangle the benefits of the hierarchical planner versus the accessibility tree grounding.

The overall dataset size is relatively small (276 total tasks), with only 51 instances in the most challenging Level-3 category, which limits statistical power when stratified across different model backends.

The manuscript cites unreleased or unverified model versions (e.g., 'GPT-5.2', 'Gemini-3.0-pro', 'Claude-Sonnet-4.5', 'Qwen3.5-397b-a17b') without clear specifications, release snapshots, or API details, impeding scientific reproducibility.

The abstract leaves the code repository URL empty ('Our code is publicly available at: .'), and the text contains clear proofreading oversights, such as verbatim duplicate sentences in the Introduction (page 1, column 2).

strengths: Addresses a fundamental challenge in GUI agent evaluation—the tension between realistic task ambiguity and verifiable deterministic ground truth—via a structured decoupling of logical causal pathways from surface linguistic instructions.

The multi-level evaluation metrics (WPSR, MATCR, p-ATSR, and error attribution) provide valuable fine-grained diagnostic insight into where and why agents fail along long-horizon execution trajectories beyond binary pass/fail rates.

The LightManus-Jarvis hierarchical framework is conceptually sound and well-engineered, demonstrating clear architectural advantages by separating macro-level dynamic context planning from micro-level hybrid (XML + screenshot) execution.
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple agent paradigms and LLM backends, complemented by an informative error analysis and significant token/runtime efficiency gains.
weaknesses: The task domain is largely limited to multi-hop factual information retrieval across knowledge-centric apps (e.g., Wikipedia, Spotify, IMDb), rather than interactive, transactional, or productivity workflows (e.g., messaging, e-commerce, device settings, forms), which restricts the ecological diversity of GUI interactions.

The benchmark size is relatively modest (276 total tasks, with only 51 in the Level-3 hard category), and scaling remains constrained by the manual verification required to validate topological paths and app interface states.

Several model backends evaluated (e.g., GPT-5.2, Gemini-3.0-Pro/Flash, Claude-Sonnet-4.5) reference unreleased or non-standard version designations without sufficient clarification of API dates, checkpoint snapshots, or exact configurations, hindering reproducibility.

The manuscript exhibits several presentation issues and drafting oversights: an incomplete URL placeholder in the Abstract, duplicated sentences in Section 1 (page 1, column 2), illegible overlapping labels in Figure 4, and identical captions ('Operational Error Example') used for Figures 7, 8, and 9 despite representing distinct error categories.
